title: The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986
explainer: The CFAA, signed into law in 1986, was the first comprehensive U.S. federal computer crime statute, and it still defines what counts as "unauthorized access" in federal court - the exact question a bug bounty program's scope language and a researcher's legal exposure both turn on. Written before the web existed, it has had to be stretched and reinterpreted since, most notably when the Supreme Court narrowed the meaning of "exceeds authorized access" in its 2021 Van Buren decision. Every safe-harbor clause in a modern disclosure policy exists largely to route good-faith researchers around the risk this one 1986 law still creates.

title: Steven Levy's "Hackers" (1984) and the Hacker Ethic
explainer: Journalist Steven Levy's 1984 book Hackers documented the informal code that grew up among MIT programmers in the 1950s and 60s - share information freely, judge people by their work, mistrust gatekeeping authority - and gave it the name "the hacker ethic." That ethic's tension between open disclosure and institutional control is the direct ancestor of today's arguments over responsible versus full disclosure, and over what a researcher who finds a flaw owes a vendor. Bug bounty programs are a comparatively recent, commercial attempt to reconcile that decades-old ethic with corporate risk management.
